background.definition: Erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease, is the most common clinical manifestation of parvovirus B19 infection. It is characterized by prodromal symptoms of fever, coryza, headache, and nausea, followed by erythema of the cheeks (slapped cheek rash) and later a maculopapular rash of the extremities and trunk.

list.listitem: The incidence of erythema infectiosum peaks in children between the ages of 4 and 10 years. In an English study, about 50% of children had seroconverted to parvovirus IgG positivity by age 15 years.
The incidence of parvovirus B19 infection among children with sickle cell disease is 11.3 per 100 patient years.
Erythema infectiosum is caused by parvovirus B19, a single-stranded DNA virus that has an affinity for rapidly dividing cell lines, such as the human erythroid progenitor cells.
Infection is spread primarily by respiratory droplets. Transmission by blood products has been documented. It may also be vertically transferred from mother to fetus.
Infection causes a rapid drop in reticulocyte count, which last for 7 to 10 days. The resulting anemia is usually not clinically apparent in healthy patients.
Parvovirus B19-specific IgM antibodies appears after clearance of the viremia.
Rash develops when parvovirus B19-specific IgG antibodies are detectable in serum, at which time patients are no longer contagious.
The demonstration of parvovirus B19 from skin biopsy suggests that there is direct involvement of the epidermal cells in the rash of erythema infectiosum.
Suspect erythema infectiosum in children with prodromal fever, coryza, headache, and nausea, followed by erythema of the cheeks. C
If testing is needed to diagnose parvovirus B19 infection in the immunocompetent patient (ie, pregnancy), order serum IgM enzyme immunoassay. C
Parvovirus B19 viral DNA testing, by PCR, is the preferred study in immunocompromised patients or those in TAC, in whom IgM or IgG antibodies may not be detectable. C

Differential.Differential_Features: May have white spots on buccal mucosa; erythematous maculopapular rash; begins on head spreads to body
Punctate rash, initially on trunk, sore throat, and cervical adenopathy tends to be present
More likely to have adenopathy and tonsillar exudates
Mucocutaneous lesions, strawberry tongue may be present, high fevers
Use anti-ds-DNA antibodies to help diagnose
Usually, history of recent drug usage

list.listitem: Parvovirus B19 infection is often asymptomatic. When symptomatic, erythema infectiosum involves 3 distinct stages: Stage 1: Prodromal illness shows cold-like symptoms, including low-grade fever, headaches, coryza, nausea, and diarrhea. Stage 2: 3 to 7 days after the prodromal period, there is the classic facial exanthem, the "slapped cheek" appearance, sparing the nasal and perioral areas. This stage may last for up to 6 weeks. Stage 3: 1 to 4 days after stage 2, there appears a lacy, maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities that usually lasts for 1 to 3 weeks.

Joint pain is common and usually involves the knees and ankles. Arthralgia was reported in 5.1% of children younger than 10 years and in 11.5% of children and adolescents between the ages of 10 and 19 years.

Other, less common presentations include thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, neurologic complications, myocarditis, and hepatitis. In a review of 98 cases of parvovirus B19 infection after transplantation, anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia were present in 98.8%, 37.5%, and 21.0% of patients, respectively.
Diagnostic testing is not needed for otherwise-healthy children with typical signs and symptoms of erythema infectiosum.

If testing is needed to diagnose parvovirus B19 infection, serum IgM enzyme immunoassay is the preferred test in the immunocompetent patient. It is 89% sensitive and 99.4% specific (LR+ 148, LR− 0.11). IgM begins to rise during the second week of illness, during the prodromal phase, and IgG begins to rise during the third week with the appearance of the rash.
Parvovirus B19-specific IgG testing is generally used to detect prior infection and immunity.
Parvovirus B19 viral DNA testing, such as by PCR, is the preferred test in the immunocompromised patients or in TAC, when patient's IgM or IgG antibodies may not be detectable.
Diagnosis of acute infection or immunity is particularly important in pregnant women, because parvovirus B19 infection is associated with pregnancy complications.
Suspect erythema infectiosum in children with prodromal fever, coryza, headache, and nausea followed by erythema of the cheeks ("slapped cheek").
Diagnostic tests are generally not recommended for immunocompetent patients, unless pregnant, in which case serum IgM enzyme immunoassay should be ordered.
PCR is a better test in patients with sickle cell anemia or immunocompromise.
Drug therapy is generally not needed in healthy children with erythema infectiosum. C
In sickle cell patients with TAC caused by parvovirus B19, blood transfusion may be required until red cell production returns. C
Immunosuppressed patients with chronic parvovirus B19 infection and anemia may benefit from commercial IV immune globulins for 5 to 10 days. B

Drug therapy is generally not needed in healthy children with erythema infectiosum, because it is self-limited. Routine supportive care with adequate oral hydration and antipyretics is generally sufficient.
Patients with parvovirus B19 infection-induced arthralgia may benefit from NSAIDs or acetaminophen for symptomatic treatment.

Sickle cell patients with TAC caused by parvovirus B19 may require blood transfusions until red cell production returns. In one study, 1 death was reported among 62 sickle cell patients with TAC, which demonstrates the potential severity of the disease in this population.

Patients with chronic parvovirus B19 infection and anemia may benefit from commercial intravenous immune globulins. Both 5 and 10 days of 400 mg/kg or 3 days of 1000 mg/kg immune globins were shown to be effective in patients with congenital immunodeficiency or HIV infection.
Intrauterine fetal blood transfusions may benefit some fetuses with hydrops fetalis resulting from parvovirus B19 infection.
Good hygiene and hand washing can help reduce transmission of parvovirus infection in the household, daycare, hospital, and school settings.
Consider hospitalization in children who have sickle cell disease or who are immunocompromised because of possible hemodynamic instability and need transfusion therapy.
Rare but serious manifestations such as myocarditis warrant admission to the hospital.
Most healthy patients with erythema multiforme have complete resolution of symptoms with no sequelae. B
The lacy, erythematous rash may last for 1 to 3 weeks and varies with exposure to heat or sunlight. B
Parvovirus B19 infection can be fatal in children with TAC. C
Patients should avoid contact with pregnant women or women attempting to become pregnant.
Use supportive therapy to keep patient well hydrated and NSAID medications for symptom relief.
Patients should follow-up with their physician if their symptoms do not improve with supportive therapy.
Patients are no longer contagious once they develop the rash of erythema infectiosum.
Parvovirus B19 infection has been associated with painful, bilateral, erythema and swelling of the feet and hands ("gloves and socks syndrome") in adults.
Supportive therapy is generally all that is needed.
30-50% of pregnant women are non-immune to parvovirus B19.
The presence of IgM or a rise in IgG antibodies indicates acute infection with parvovirus B19.
Serial ultrasonography is recommended. If hydrops fetalis develops, blood transfusion may be necessary.
Fetuses at highest risk for disease should undergo weekly doppler examination of the middle cerebral artery.

A meta-analysis based on 10 cases in Japan and on previous cases reported in the literature indicated that parvovirus B19 was responsible for 15% to 20% of cases of nonimmune hydrops fetalis. A study of 63 pregnant women with parvovirus B19 found a 31.7% vertical transmission to the fetus. Parvovivus B19 during pregnancy was associated with a 71% increased risk of fetal loss (OR: 1.7; 95% CI: 1.02-2.86).
One large study found that intrauterine transfusion in parvovirus B19 caused fetal hydrops reduced in utero death rate from 30% to 6%.
One case report illustrated that parvovirus B19 can cause a congenital infection syndrome evident by cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly, profound anemia, and a purple papulonodular "blueberry-muffin" rash.
